While lithium-ion batteries currently lead in performance, Adelhelm described sodium-ion technology as “the only viable competitor that we have right now,” arguing that both technologies could complement each other across different applications, particularly where cost and material availability matter.

He identified lithium prices as a major factor in sodium-ion adoption, observing that “the higher the lithium price, the more attractive it is to look at alternatives.” Sodium’s abundance could also reduce environmental impacts associated with sourcing raw materials.

Adelhelm identified stationary energy storage as a promising market for sodium-ion batteries. He also sees opportunities to compete with lead-acid batteries, citing better energy density and low-temperature performance, although their precise role in the wider battery market remains uncertain.

Doctors corrected a single wrong letter of DNA inside patients' livers, and their bodies started making a missing protective protein again.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is an inherited disorder: one misplaced DNA "letter" means the liver makes a faulty version of a protein that protects the lungs. It can lead to emphysema and cirrhosis, and is often mistaken for asthma.

A Hannover Medical School team and Renji Hospital in Shanghai used base editing, a CRISPR-based tool that swaps one letter without cutting both DNA strands, delivered by a single infusion. Seven patients were treated in Shanghai. One 55-year-old, who had needed weekly protein infusions, has made working protein again since March with no side effects reported and no longer needs those infusions.

Limits: early safety-and-efficacy results in a small group (Journal of Hepatology), funded by the Chinese company that holds the patents; not approved; it cannot undo lung or liver damage already done. A trial at Hannover is planned for early 2027.

Source: https://t.co/DS5VLxcvTP

In Vivo Ep. 47 Companion Article, by Dr. Tim Gabor
Watch the full episode: Editing Embryos: The Biotech Frontier That Changes Everything | Cathy Tie and Prof. Jiang | Ep. 47
Every so often a conversation lands on In Vivo that I know will split the comment section down the middle. Episode 47 was one of them. I sat down with Cathy Tie, founder of Origin Genomics, and Prof. Jiang Xueqin of Predictive History, two fellow Torontonians who come at biotech from opposite directions. Cathy is building a company to correct disease-causing mutations in human embryos. Prof. Jiang spends his time thinking about power, history and game theory. Put them in the same room and you get the science, the ethics and the geopolitics of germline editing all at once.
This piece is for those who prefer the written word, and for anyone who wants the key ideas, the papers and a few of the best moments in one place.
Reading DNA vs. writing DNA
Cathy's path into science started early. She published her first peer-reviewed paper as a teenager (Tie, 2013, Canadian Young Scientist Journal) and went on to found companies during the direct-to-consumer genetics boom. Her framing for where the field has gone is simple: for decades we got very good at reading DNA. Now we are learning to write it.
The landmark moment for writing DNA in the clinic came in December 2023, when the FDA approved Casgevy, the first CRISPR-based therapy, for sickle cell disease (FDA announcement). It is a genuine triumph. It is also a somatic therapy, meaning the edit lives in the patient's own blood stem cells and is not passed on to their children.
 
Somatic vs. germline, and why the embryo matters
Early in the episode I asked Cathy to lay out the difference. Her answer is the clearest one-paragraph primer I have heard:
"There's two types of cells in a human body. There's somatic cells and germline cells. Somatic cells are anything that's not reproduction related and germline cells are anything reproduction related. So sperm, egg, embryos."
The reason she is working at the embryo stage is not philosophical, it is practical. The biggest bottleneck in adult gene therapy is delivery. An adult has trillions of cells, and the editing machinery has to reach the right ones. That usually means packaging it in a viral vector such as an AAV. As I said on the show, people hear "virus" and panic, but viruses are an everyday lab tool precisely because delivering DNA into cells is what they evolved to do. Still, the vector brings risk and cost. In Cathy's words:
"If you look at all the failures with gene therapies, especially recently and in clinical trials where these gene therapies have failed, it's mostly, if not all, due to the virus negatively impacting the patient."
Her point: an embryo solves the delivery problem. Correct the mutation in a single cell before it starts dividing, and every daughter cell inherits the fix.
"You can actually design these gene editors to go directly into the embryo and correct that mutation before the cell starts dividing into two, four, eight, hundreds, thousands and then millions and billions."
 
That is also exactly what makes germline editing different. The correction is heritable. It goes to the next generation, and the next, and the next. That is the promise and the reason for caution in the same sentence.
Where this plugs into IVF
One thing I appreciated is that Cathy does not pitch this as replacing IVF. She pitches it as an add-on. Today, a family carrying a known mutation can do preimplantation genetic testing (PGT): screen the embryos, discard the ones carrying the mutation, implant the healthy ones. The problem is the numbers game. People going through IVF are often older and may only have a handful of viable embryos. Correction, in her view, gives them more options instead of fewer embryos.
She also reminded us that IVF itself went through the same panic. When Robert Edwards and colleagues brought it into the world, the press reached for "Frankenstein" and "test tube babies." Edwards went on to win the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, and millions of people alive today were conceived by IVF. Whether germline editing follows the same arc is the open question.
Base editors and the safety question
The loudest objection to embryo editing has always been safety. Classic CRISPR-Cas9 works by cutting both strands of DNA, and the cell's repair of that break can go wrong: off-target edits, large deletions, chromosomal abnormalities, mosaic embryos. That is a big part of why the 2018 He Jiankui affair, where twin girls were born after their embryos were edited to disable the CCR5 gene, triggered global condemnation and a prison sentence (Nature news).
Newer tools change the conversation. Base editors swap a single DNA letter without a double-strand break, and prime editors can write small corrections more precisely still. Cathy pointed to a June 2026 preprint from a Columbia group (Egli lab) reporting efficient base editing in human embryos without the chromosomal alterations that dogged earlier work (bioRxiv preprint; C&EN coverage).
In fairness to the science, I want to flag the caveat. That Columbia work did not correct disease mutations, and the authors themselves still describe clinical use as premature. Cathy's on-air summary was more upbeat than the paper's conclusion, which is the kind of gap worth keeping in mind as this field heats up.
Origin Genomics, she told me, operates an IRB-approved lab working with donated human embryos that carry disease mutations, testing base and prime editors on them. Her stated first focus is hereditary cancers, followed by well-characterized single-gene conditions like Huntington's. Since we recorded, the paper she mentioned on the show has come out: "No bird soars in a calm: therapeutic germline gene editing" in Trends in Genetics (published online Sept 30, 2026), arguing for rigorous preclinical data and a new regulatory pathway beginning with severe monogenic disease. For the critical view, The Scientist and WIRED both covered the pushback.
Therapy vs. enhancement: can you even draw the line?
I asked Cathy where she draws it. Her answer: correction means fixing a mutation that is known, with a large body of literature behind it, to cause disease. Anything else is inducing a variant that did not need to be there. She was firm that choice has to sit with families, given the dark history of eugenics:
"I want to help hundreds of millions of people not pass down their genetic disease if they choose not to."
Prof. Jiang was not convinced the line holds. His take was the sharpest moment of the episode:
"If you're able to correct you can also enhance... once you have the technology in place you open Pandora's box and I think it'll be really hard to regulate especially given that science is transnational."
As a molecular biologist, I will add one point I made on the show. Most traits are multifactorial, many genes playing together like a symphony. That is precisely why the first targets are monogenic diseases, where one well-defined variant does the damage. Enhancement of complex traits like intelligence is, scientifically, a far harder problem than headlines suggest. Prof. Jiang's warning is less about the biology today and more about incentives tomorrow.
The US, China and who builds the biotech century
Cathy's read is that China excels at going from one to one hundred, and the US at going from zero to one. Biotech, she argued, is different from the internet, because a therapy that works here works everywhere. You cannot wall it off the way you can build a local search engine.
Prof. Jiang described decades of quiet US-China cooperation in human genetics that, as he put it, "transcends the nation state rivalry," and an especially techno-utopian culture in China, built on a generation that watched technology lift the country out of poverty. You do not have to agree with every geopolitical prediction to see his core point: if one country forbids something and another permits it, the rules can end up being set by whoever is most permissive.
Gene drives and the game theory of biology
The last third of the conversation got darker, in a useful way. Cathy brought up gene drives, the technology behind efforts such as the Gates-backed Target Malaria project. Normal Mendelian inheritance passes a variant to roughly half of offspring. A gene drive biases inheritance so that nearly all offspring carry it, allowing a trait to sweep through a wild population (Nature primer on gene drives).
 
Her concern was simple: "these mosquitoes don't respect borders." Then she compared biotech to the Manhattan Project. A nuclear weapon needs a facility, and when one is fired, you know where it came from. Biology is different:
"It actually is more dangerous from a game theory perspective than atomic bombs because you don't know where it's coming from... and more people can get access to it."
That led me to recommend Annie Jacobsen's Biological War, and Cathy revealed she had been interviewed for it. Small world.
My take
I left this conversation with two thoughts that are both true at once. First, the medical case for correcting a devastating single-gene mutation at the embryo stage is real, and the tools are better than they were in 2018. Second, the hardest problems here are not technical. They are about oversight, incentives and who gets to decide. Cathy is betting that transparent, IRB-reviewed science in the US is the responsible path. Prof. Jiang is betting that once the box is open, the rules will be written by whoever moves fastest.
My advice to students listening: learn the biology deeply enough that you can tell a base editor from a gene drive, and a monogenic disease from a polygenic trait. That literacy is the only way to have this debate honestly.
Watch the full conversation here: In Vivo Ep. 47 on YouTube. Find Cathy at @CathyTie and Prof. Jiang at Predictive History.
See you In Vivo.

TSMC'nin Ekim Geliri %59,7 Arttı, AI Çiplerinde Darboğaz Paketleme Hattında

10 Kasım'da TSMC Ekim gelirini açıkladı: 586,89 milyar Tayvan doları. Bu, bir yıl öncesine göre %59,7, yalnızca bir ay öncesine göre ise %14,7 artış demek. Manşet AI talebinin sürdüğünü söylüyor. Ama rakamın altındaki mesele, fabrikanın kaç wafer bastığından çok basılan die'ların ne hızla tek bir pakette birleştirilebildiği. CEO C. C. Wei, Ekim ortasındaki bilanço toplantısında sıkıntının yerini açıkça gösterdi: "back-end tarafında biraz sıkıntımız var."

Sıkıntının adı CoWoS. TSMC'nin AI hızlandırıcılarını paketlediği bu hattın kapasitesinin 2027 sonuna kadar dolu olduğu bildiriliyor. En büyük rezervasyonların NVIDIA (NVDA), AMD ve Google'da bulunduğu, paketleme teslim sürelerinin de uzadığı haberler arasında. 8 Ekim'de TSMC, CoWoS'un silikon katmanı için GlobalFoundries'le 2 milyar dolarlık bir tedarik anlaşması imzaladı. Ekim sonunda ise şirketin CoWoS fiyatlarını %20'ye kadar artırmayı tarttığı bildirildi; TSMC bunu doğrulamadı. Üç gelişme birlikte okununca kıt olanın yalnızca ileri süreç wafer'ı olmadığı görülüyor. O wafer'dan çıkan çipleri bir sisteme dönüştüren paket de sıraya girmiş durumda.

CoWoS nedir?

Bir litografi makinesi tek pozlamada en fazla bir reticle, yani ~830 mm² alan basabilir. Tek bir die bu sınırı aşamaz. Oysa bugünün AI hızlandırıcısı birden fazla compute die ile bunların yanına dizilen HBM stack'lerinden oluşuyor. HBM4'te her stack işlemciyle 2048 bitlik bir arayüzden konuşuyor; HBM3E'de bu 1024 bitti. Bu kadar paralel hattı, çipin karta oturduğu organik substrate taşıyamaz, çünkü hatları bu yoğunluk için fazla kaba.

CoWoS (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate) araya ikinci bir silikon katman koyuyor: wafer litografisiyle üretilen ve PCB'nin çizemeyeceği incelikte bakır hatlar taşıyan bir interposer. Sinyalin yolu şöyle: compute die → mikro bump → interposer içindeki ince hatlar → yan yana duran HBM stack'inin base die'ı. Güç ve dış dünyaya giden sinyaller ise interposer'ı dikine delen TSV'lerden (silikon içi geçiş) substrate'e, oradan da karta iniyor. Ad süreci anlatıyor. Önce die'lar henüz wafer hâlindeki interposer'a dizilir (CoW), sonra bütün yapı substrate'e oturtulur (oS).

Sorun ölçek. Tam silikon interposer kullanan CoWoS-S, 2016'da 1,5 reticle boyutundaydı ve 2023'te 3,3'e çıktı; silikon büyüdükçe maliyet de büyüdü. CoWoS-L silikonu yalnızca gereken yere koyuyor. Die'ların birbirine baktığı kenarlara küçük LSI (yerel silikon bağlantı) köprüleri gömülüyor, geri kalan alanı daha ucuz RDL (yeniden dağıtım katmanı) taşıyor. Bugün 5,5 reticle boyutunda üretim yapılıyor. 2028 için ise yaklaşık 10 büyük compute die ile 20 HBM stack'ini tek pakete toplayan 14 reticle planlanıyor. Wei bugünkü boyuttaki üretimi TSMC'ye özgü görüyor: "Bugün bunu Taiwan Semiconductor dışında kimsenin yapabildiğine inanmıyorum."

Artısı: Bant genişliği yoğunluğu ve kısa yol. Paket artık reticle sınırına takılmıyor; sistem tek bir die'da değil, pakette kuruluyor.

Bedeli: Üç kalem. Verim (yield): Birden çok pahalı die ve HBM tek pakette birleşiyor. Mikro bump hassasiyeti verimi doğrudan belirliyor ve montajdaki bir hata hepsini birden harcayabilir. Geometri: Büyük dikdörtgen interposer'lar yuvarlak wafer'ın kenarını boşa harcıyor. TSMC bu yüzden 310×310 mm'lik paneller kullanan CoPoS'u deniyor, ama hacimli üretimin 2028'in ikinci yarısından önce beklenmediği bildiriliyor. Test: Paket büyüdükçe son testin de belirgin biçimde uzadığı bildiriliyor.

Kısaca: transistörü wafer üretiyor, sistemi paket kuruyor. İleri paketlemenin TSMC gelirindeki payı 2025'te ~%8'di; bu yıl %10'un biraz üzerine çıkması bekleniyor.

Zincirde kim ne yapıyor?

TSMC — kapının sahibi. Zincirin litografi isteyen kısmı, yani interposer, LSI köprüleri ve CoW aşaması TSMC'de.

ASE (ASX) — back-end'in hacim oyuncusu. Zincirin montaj ve test halkasındaki OSAT (dış kaynaklı montaj ve test şirketi). İleri paketleme ve test gelirinin (LEAP) 2026'da 4 milyar dolara ulaşması bekleniyor. Tahmin 3,7 milyardan yükseltildi ve bu kalemin 2027'de ikiye katlanması öngörülüyor.

Amkor (AMKR) — Amerika'daki yedek kapı. Arizona'da ileri paketleme ve test kampüsü kuruyor, ama AI dalgası ona henüz sınırlı dokunuyor. Üçüncü çeyrek geliri 1,99 milyar dolarla bir yıl öncesiyle aynı kaldı; 2,5D paketlemedeki büyüme telefon tarafındaki zayıflığı ancak dengeledi.

GlobalFoundries (GFS) — interposer taşeronu. Beş yıllık anlaşmayla New York'taki Malta fabrikasında CoWoS için silikon interposer üretecek. Hacimli üretimin 2028'in ilk yarısında başlaması planlanıyor ve fabrikanın ABD'deki ilk interposer kaynağı olması bekleniyor.

Intel (INTC) — kapının yanındaki yol. EMIB büyük bir interposer kullanmıyor, köprü die'ını doğrudan substrate'in içine gömüyor. Google'ın bir sonraki TPU neslinde bu yola yöneldiği bildiriliyor. Intel'in finans direktörü David Zinsner EMIB için şöyle konuşuyor: "yılda milyarlarca dolar düzeyindeki bazı anlaşmaları kapatmaya yakınız." Bu gelir gerçekleşirse bir kısmı, TSMC'de bu yıl gelirin %10'unun biraz üzerine çıkması beklenen ileri paketleme kaleminden kayan iş olabilir. Müşteri wafer'ı TSMC'de bastırıp paketi Intel'e götürebiliyorsa wafer geliri yerinde kalabilir, ama paketlemenin müşteriyi wafer'a bağlama gücü zayıflar. Wei de rakibi küçümsemiyor: "rakibimiz çok rekabetçi bir çözüm sunuyor." Ardından ekliyor: "şimdilik CoWoS hâlâ müşterilerimizin bir numaralı tercihi."

Kâr havuzunu kim topluyor?

AI çipini iki kapılı bir hat gibi düşünün. Birinci kapı wafer: transistör orada basılıyor. İkinci kapı paket: die'lar ve HBM orada bir sisteme dönüşüyor. Eskiden ikinci kapı, fabrikadan çıkan çipin düşük marjlı montaj şirketlerine gittiği son adım sayılırdı. CoWoS bu ayrımı yeniden çizdi. Litografi isteyen kısım foundry'de toplandı, emek ve hacim isteyen kısım OSAT'ta kaldı.

Marjlar bu ayrımı ancak dolaylı gösteriyor. ASE'nin brüt marjı üçüncü çeyrekte rekor seviyeye, %22,1'e çıktı; TSMC'nin şirket geneli brüt marjı aynı çeyrekte %66,41'di. TSMC paketlemenin marjını ayrı açıklamıyor; bu oran ağırlıkla wafer işini yansıtıyor. Paketleme TSMC gelirinin yalnızca yaklaşık onda biri, ama müşteri paketi başka yerde yaptıramadığı sürece onu en ileri wafer'a bağlayan halka. Bu halkanın dokunduğu gelir küçük değil: AI hızlandırıcılarının da içinde bulunduğu, ama tamamı CoWoS'a bağlı olmayan HPC segmenti üçüncü çeyrekte TSMC gelirinin %68'ini oluşturdu. Kapı dar kaldıkça fiyat üzerinde söz hakkı da kapıyı tutanda olur. Yine de konuşulan %20'lik CoWoS artışının tamamı bile satışlara ancak ~%2 ekleyebilir. Asıl kazanç, kapıdan geçen müşterinin wafer'ını da TSMC'de bastırması olabilir. Yatırımcı dilinde: TSMC paketlemeyi ayrı bir kâr merkezi gibi değil, wafer gelirini kilitleyen bir geçiş noktası gibi işletiyor görünüyor.

Boğa (tema): Birincisi silikon yoğunluğu. 5,5 reticle'dan 14 reticle'a giden yol, her pakette daha çok compute die ve HBM demek; her adım hem wafer hem paketleme geliri doğurabilir. İkincisi fiyatlama gücü. Kapasitenin dolu olduğu bildiriliyor ve fiyat artışı konuşuluyor. Üçüncüsü kapasite. Aylık CoWoS kapasitesinin 2028 sonuna kadar yaklaşık iki katına çıkarılmasının planlandığı bildiriliyor; talep sürerse bu genişleme gelire dönüşebilir.

Ayı (tema): Birincisi alternatif kapılar. Intel'in EMIB'i, OSAT kapasitesi ve TSMC'nin kendi panel geçişi kapıyı genişletiyor; kapı genişledikçe geçiş ücreti düşebilir. İkincisi kapasite döngüsü. İkiye katlanan bir CoWoS hattı, AI yatırım harcaması yavaşlarsa boş kalabilir. Üçüncüsü karmaşıklık. 14 reticle'lık bir pakette tek kusurun bedeli büyüyor ve test süreleri uzuyor; bu da maliyeti ve teslim takvimini zorlayabilir.

Bunu belirleyecek üç değişken var: 9 reticle CoWoS'un üretime giriş takvimi, Google'ın EMIB'li TPU'sunun hacme çıkıp çıkmadığı ve TSMC'nin konuşulan CoWoS fiyat artışını 14 Ocak 2027'deki bilançoda doğrulayıp doğrulamadığı.

The industry is obsessed with GPU compute capabilities, but the actual choke point of the AI revolution isn't just printing the silicon. It's packaging it.

We have hit the reticle limit—the physical maximum size a monolithic chip can be manufactured. To scale further, modern AI accelerators rely on "Advanced Packaging" (like TSMC's CoWoS). 

Instead of printing one massive die, foundries physically stitch together multiple smaller "chiplets" alongside High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) stacks on a microscopic silicon interposer. This requires aligning tens of thousands of microscopic copper microbumps with absolute zero margin for error. 

The global bottleneck for AI infrastructure is the raw capacity of these advanced packaging facilities. You can print millions of raw chips, but if you can't attach them to HBM at scale, you have no AI accelerators.

Software engineers must internalize this: hardware scaling is now heavily constrained by the physics of thermal expansion and microscopic packaging. Algorithmic efficiency (quantization, efficient attention) isn't just a cost-saving measure; it is the only way to bypass the physical packaging bottleneck.

一、为什么TSMC很重要
双方从1997年Riva128开始合作，近30年，特点不是一纸长期垄断大单，而是同步联合研发、优先产能、先进封装深度绑定：CoWoS先进封装是高端AI卡的刚需：H100、Blackwell都高度依赖台积电CoWoS，用来把GPU、HBM封装在一起，实现超高带宽；这个工艺不是单纯代工，是英伟达和台积电提前好几年对齐需求、一起调良率的结果。没有CoWoS，高端AI芯片性能会直接大打折扣。
优先锁定先进节点与产能：AI爆发后先进制程、CoWoS产能极度稀缺；基于长期信任，英伟达可以提前下巨额产能承诺，拿到优先排产权，保证迭代节奏不被卡断。黄仁勋自己提到，双方很多时候不靠严格合同，靠长期信任、“大致公平”的默契，敢互相押注、一起承担新工艺风险。

如果台积电是决定性因素，那么苹果、AMD、高通同样用台积电，就应该复制英伟达的AI统治地位。英伟达真正的底层壁垒是：CUDA软件生态：二十年积累，海量算子、框架、论文、工程师习惯绑定在CUDA上。硬件参数可以追上，但迁移成本极高，这是最核心护城河。
全栈能力：不止GPU芯片，还有NVLink互联、网络、整机方案、软件库、配套工程团队，给云厂商、大模型公司做端到端调优，卖的是算力系统，不是单独一块芯片。
黄仁勋对AI趋势的判断+全产业链调度能力：不止台积电，他同样很早就推动HBM厂商扩产、服务器供应链配套，是在调度一整个算力产业链，而不只是和代工厂搞好关系。

सेमीकंडक्टर मुख्य रूप से सिलिकॉन जैसे पदार्थों से बनाए जाते हैं, जिनकी विद्युत चालकता नियंत्रित की जा सकती है।

$NVDA 不是一家孤零零的公司，它是整条AI半导体产业链的指挥中心。黄仁勋这一走，受影响的远不止一只股票。

先把这条链子理清楚，跟$NVDA有关的，基本可以分成七层。

第一层，造芯片的。$NVDA自己不生产芯片，所有GPU都由$TSM代工，从最先进的制程到CoWoS先进封装，全压在$TSM身上。可以说，$TSM的产能有多少，$NVDA就能卖多少。

第二层，内存。每一颗AI芯片旁边都堆着一圈HBM，供应商是SK Hynix、Samsung和$MU。一代GPU的性能能往上跳多少，很大程度上看HBM跟不跟得上。这两年存储变成了AI的新瓶颈，背后就是$NVDA一代代往上加HBM的用量。

第三层，设备和设计软件。$TSM和内存厂要扩产，就得买$ASML的光刻机，买$AMAT、$LRCX、$KLAC的设备。芯片在设计阶段，又离不开$SNPS和$CDNS的EDA工具。$NVDA的订单，一层层传导成了这些公司的订单。

第四层，网络和光。一个机柜里72颗GPU要连在一起，一个数据中心里几万颗也要连在一起，靠的是NVLink、交换机、光模块和高速线缆。$NVDA自己做了一部分，$COHR、$CRDO、$APH这些公司吃的是剩下的那块。$AVGO和$ANET则是一边合作，一边竞争。

第五层，整机和机房。$DELL、$SMCI把芯片装成服务器和整机柜，$VRT做液冷和供电，$ETN做配电。现在一个机柜功率越来越高，这一层的重要性也越来越大。

第六层，客户。$MSFT、$META、$GOOGL、$AMZN、$ORCL是最大的买家，$CRWV、$NBIS这些新云靠借钱买卡。这些钱最后大头流回$NVDA，再从$NVDA流向上面那几层。

第七层，是$NVDA自己投出去的生态。它投了$CRWV，入股了$INTC，跟OpenAI签了大单，还在一堆AI创业公司里有股份。用钱把需求和供应两头都绑在自己身上。

这七层，是谁在拧成一股绳？

黄仁勋。

$TSM的产能要提前好几年锁，内存要提前跟厂家定规格，光模块、液冷、电源都得按$NVDA的路线图同步升级。一年一代新架构，几十家供应商要跟着一起跑，任何一家掉链子，整个节奏就乱了。

这些年$TSM的CoWoS产能为什么优先给$NVDA，HBM规格为什么跟着$NVDA走，整机柜方案为什么能这么快推开，很大程度上靠的是黄仁勋这个人。他自己飞去台湾谈产能，自己站台定路线，自己在GTC上把下一代的需求讲给全世界听。

供应商敢扩产，客户敢下单，资本市场敢给估值，三方面的信心都押在他身上。

没了黄仁勋怎么办？

短期，订单不会消失。客户已经下的单要交付，$TSM的产能也排好了，下周的财报大概率依然很好看。

可接下来的几年，问题就来了。

下一代架构的取舍谁来拍板？跟$TSM、内存厂抢产能谁去谈？客户被$AMD和自研芯片拉走的时候，谁去把他们留住？这些事，靠一个临时CEO兼CFO是撑不住的。

更麻烦的是，整条链子都在跟着$NVDA的路线图扩产。旗手换人，路线图可能放慢，可能改方向，上游那些砸了几百亿扩产能的公司，心里也会开始打鼓。

所以我的看法很直接：订单还在，但整条半导体产业链的确定性，已经跟着黄仁勋一起打了折扣。

这时候更要看清楚，产业链上谁离$NVDA最近，谁的客户最分散。$TSM和存储的客户不止$NVDA一家，受的冲击会小一些。那些靠$NVDA一个大客户吃饭的，风险就大得多。

我的做法不变：不上杠杆，不追反弹，按价位分批，等新CEO的人选和下周的财报出来，再一家一家重新评估。

A lot of people I speak to in India don't realise the significance of the Jensen Huang affair. If anything, it shows the importance of sovereign AI.

We all know about the affair. But that is the least interesting part of this story.

This is about Chinese AI, and how the Americans are successfully reducing China's AI capability.

People look at DeepSeek and other Chinese open-source models and feel that China is very close to the US in AI. In terms of the models, that is true. But in terms of the AI infrastructure layer, China has been deeply curtailed by the US.

We have all heard about the US chip controls on China. What do they mean? They mean that not just Nvidia, but Dutch companies like ASML, Korean companies like SK Hynix and Samsung, and TSMC are not allowed to export their most advanced products to China.

Think about it. The chip industry's supply chain today covers the entire globe:

→ The chip designers in the US
→ The EUV machines in the Netherlands
→ The memory makers in Korea
→ The wafer supply chain in Japan
→ The most famous fab in the world in Taiwan

Each of these parts is incredibly complicated and hard. So much so that no single country is able to do it all. Each specialises in its own sphere, and the industry coordinates like one big family across the globe.

It was famously noted that Nvidia and TSMC didn't have a contract. They had an understanding. Because they know they can't function without each other.

Effectively, the Americans are asking China to build the entire supply chain in its own country.

There is a myth that China will be able to do this easily. People in the chip industry know that making 3-nanometre AI chips end to end is harder than making a rocket. It is the hardest thing humans have ever produced.

So China is trying its best, and has achieved great results. But it is still some way behind the US.

It has DUV machines, not EUV machines. It's not able to make HBM at scale, the memory that sits extremely close to the processor in an AI chip. And it's not able to make 3-nanometre processor chips.

The result is that China is adding seven to eight times as much new power as the US every year, and still lagging behind in data centres. SemiAnalysis estimates about 56 GW of data-centre capacity in the US by the end of 2026, against about 24 GW in China. Epoch AI says 72% of the world's AI compute since 2022 has gone to the US and about 10% to China. In the first half of 2026, the US took 78% of the new compute.

SemiAnalysis says China's build-out is held back by chips, not by land or power.

Probably this is why they went so hard to smuggle Nvidia chips. The Information reports the affair helped move at least $7.5 billion of them to Chinese firms. None of that is proven yet, and China calls it groundless. But this is why it's such a big deal for the US.

TECH IDEA | November 11, 2026

THE 230-FOLD GAP

On November 5, IBM, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, and AMD announced infrastructure that sounds dull until you read the numbers. They are putting IBM's most powerful quantum processor, the 120-qubit Nighthawk, in the same facility as Oak Ridge's Umbra supercomputer, a system built on AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and fifth-generation EPYC CPUs. The goal is a faster repair loop, not a bigger calculation.

Quantum computers are noisy. A qubit holds its state for a short time, and every operation risks corrupting it. Error correction spreads one logical qubit across many physical ones and checks them constantly, while the calculation is still running. Measure a qubit mid-circuit, decode the error, and adjust the next pulse before the information decays. That loop is where most quantum roadmaps stall, and it is mostly a classical computing problem.

That is why the machine next door matters. Umbra supplies the classical muscle to test decoding schemes at scale: concatenated codes against space-time codes, algorithm-aware decoders, hardware-aware compilation. Nighthawk's square-lattice layout and real-time pulse control let researchers measure qubits mid-calculation and act on the result.

The yardstick comes from the Department of Energy's Quantum Genesis Mission. Its Q Competition asks for 100 logical qubits running 100,000 hard operations by late 2028. IBM's current mark, tracked publicly on its Quantum Advantage Tracker, is 70 logical qubits and 438 hard operations. Closing the gap means roughly a 230-fold increase in operations, while the qubit count is already close.

IBM research chief Jay Gambetta put it plainly: "The question is no longer if error correction will work on quantum hardware. Today, the question is how to accelerate and optimize error correction to build systems that scientists can use to tackle meaningful problems."

A few things this announcement is not. It is not a new fidelity record, and no performance numbers have come out of the platform itself. There is no product, no funding figure, and no timeline for when results go public. What it is: a testbed for learning which classical resources actually shrink decoder latency and sample overhead.

The next machine on IBM's roadmap, the fault-tolerant Starling, depends on answers this platform is built to produce. Quantum computing has spent a decade proving qubits can work. The work now is proving they can keep working, long enough to matter, with a supercomputer standing next to them doing the repairs.

 QUANTUM COMPUTING & CAPITAL MARKETS

QUANTUM HARDWARE CLEARED THE TECHNICAL BAR. REVENUE MISSED THE COMMERCIAL ONE.

Quantum computing is making measurable technological progress.

But the distance between scientific achievement and commercial profitability remains substantial.

Rigetti Computing reported that its 108-qubit quantum system achieved 99.5% median two-qubit gate fidelity.

The result meets a technical objective established earlier this year.

Yet the company's third-quarter revenue totaled just $1.4 million, falling approximately 28% from the previous year and substantially missing analyst expectations.

The contrast reveals an important challenge facing the emerging quantum computing industry.

Improving the technology is one milestone.

Building a sustainable business around that technology is another.

🟨 WHAT CHANGED

🟢 Rigetti achieved 99.5% median two-qubit gate fidelity on its 108-qubit Cepheus system.

🟢 The improvement follows the 99.1% performance reported when the system became generally available in April.

🟢 The architecture combines twelve interconnected nine-qubit chiplets.

🔴 Third-quarter revenue declined approximately 28% to $1.4 million.

🔴 Revenue fell substantially below expectations of approximately $3.7 million.

🔴 Quarterly operating losses reached $33.2 million.

🟢 The company ended September with $497.1 million in cash and investments and no debt.

🟡 Management expects approximately $20 million in full-year revenue, dependent partly on customer acceptance of a system during the fourth quarter.

The hardware is advancing.

The commercial business remains at an earlier stage.

🟨 THE FIDELITY MILESTONE

Quantum computers use qubits to process information through quantum mechanical operations.

Unlike conventional computers, quantum systems face unusual challenges involving noise, environmental disturbances and computational errors.

Improving the reliability of quantum operations is therefore essential.

Rigetti's latest result demonstrates progress.

Its 108-qubit system achieved 99.5% median two-qubit gate fidelity.

That compares with 99.1% when the system became generally available earlier this year.

The improvement is meaningful because the company is attempting to maintain system performance while operating a processor containing more than 100 physical qubits.

But fidelity measures must be interpreted carefully.

A 99.5% median fidelity does not mean every operation succeeds with that probability under every workload.

Nor does it establish that the system can perform commercially useful calculations beyond the capabilities of classical computers.

The technical achievement is real.

Its eventual economic significance remains to be demonstrated.

🟨 WHY THE CHIPLET ARCHITECTURE MATTERS

Rigetti's processor uses twelve interconnected nine-qubit chiplets.

This modular approach attempts to address one of the central engineering challenges in quantum computing.

Scaling.

Increasing the number of qubits can create additional problems involving calibration, fabrication consistency and unwanted interactions.

A modular architecture could make it easier to manufacture and connect smaller components into larger systems.

But scalability requires more than adding qubits.

The system must preserve reliability as the architecture expands.

That is why improvements in fidelity matter.

The number of physical qubits alone does not determine the usefulness of a quantum computer.

Performance, error correction, connectivity and computational capability all contribute to the broader picture.

🟨 THE COMMERCIAL DIVIDE

Rigetti's financial results demonstrate how early the industry remains.

Quarterly revenue totaled $1.4 million.

Operating losses reached $33.2 million.

The company continues investing in engineering, manufacturing and research capabilities ahead of widespread commercial adoption.

Its full-year revenue outlook also depends partly on customer acceptance of a quantum computing system.

That introduces another important distinction.

Technology development does not automatically produce revenue.

Customer acceptance, contractual delivery obligations and accounting recognition determine when revenue enters the financial statements.

The industry may eventually support substantial commercial applications.

But the current financial scale remains limited.

Investors must distinguish long term technological potential from near term operating performance.

🟨 THE GOVERNMENT FUNDING DIMENSION

Public funding remains an important part of the quantum computing investment landscape.

In September, Rigetti signed an agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce providing for up to $100 million in research and development support.

The arrangement also included a minority government equity interest.

The funding supports research involving control electronics, cryogenic infrastructure and advanced chip fabrication.

These are important technical foundations.

But research funding should not be confused with broad commercial demand.

Government support can help advance emerging technologies before private markets develop sufficiently to finance them independently.

That support does not guarantee future customer adoption or shareholder profitability.

🟨 THE NEXT COMMERCIAL TEST

Rigetti is targeting larger systems with higher reliability over the coming years.

The company's roadmap includes a system exceeding 300 qubits, with improved fidelity, by mid 2028.

Longer term objectives extend toward approximately 1,000 qubits and integrated error correction capabilities.

These are management targets, not completed achievements.

The question is whether future systems can deliver useful computational advantages at an economically attractive cost.

That requires progress in several areas.

Hardware performance.

Error correction.

Manufacturing scalability.

Software integration.

Customer adoption.

And revenue generation.

A commercially viable quantum computing business must eventually combine those capabilities.

🟨 THE INVESTMENT DISTINCTION

Quantum computing shares represent exposure to a developing technology with considerable uncertainty.

Positive research results can strengthen confidence in an engineering approach.

But investment valuations also depend on future revenue, operating costs, financing requirements and the timing of commercial adoption.

Those expectations can change rapidly.

A company may achieve an important technical milestone while simultaneously reporting disappointing financial results.

Both developments can be true.

The technology may be progressing.

The business model may still be searching for scale.

🟨 WHAT SNF IS WATCHING

Further improvements in two-qubit gate fidelity.

Performance across larger physical qubit systems.

Progress toward practical error correction.

Independent evidence of useful computational advantages.

Customer acceptance of the C-DAC system.

Actual fourth quarter revenue recognition.

Government research funding and associated conditions.

Operating cash consumption.

Research and manufacturing expenses.

Competition across superconducting, trapped-ion and neutral-atom architectures.

Expansion of commercial customer relationships.

And whether improving quantum hardware performance begins translating into repeatable revenue.

🟢 SIGNAL: Rigetti achieved its 99.5% fidelity objective on a 108-qubit system, strengthening evidence of progress in its modular hardware architecture.

⚪ NOISE: Treating higher physical qubit counts or improved fidelity as proof of immediate commercial quantum advantage.

🔴 RISK: Limited revenue, continuing operating losses, uncertain commercialization timelines and rapid technological competition could constrain financial returns.

🟨 THE BOTTOM LINE

Quantum computing continues advancing toward more capable hardware.

Rigetti's latest results provide measurable evidence of that progress.

Its processor achieved a previously established fidelity target.

But quarterly revenue declined and operating losses remained substantial.

The distinction matters.

Technical progress creates possibilities.

The next stage of quantum computing will not be measured by qubit counts alone.

IBM + AMD + Oak Ridge: quantum and supercomputing brief
Current as of November 12, 2026
Executive summary
IBM, AMD, and Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) have launched a research platform that pairs an IBM quantum processor with an AMD-powered high-performance computing system. The first use is quantum error correction: testing how classical computers can detect and correct errors quickly enough to make quantum processors more reliable.
The platform is co-located at IBM’s site in Poughkeepsie, New York, and connected to ORNL’s wider supercomputing ecosystem. It is a step toward integrating quantum processors, CPUs, GPUs, and large supercomputers into shared scientific workflows. Its immediate purpose is research and system development; the launch announcement reports no end-to-end scientific speedup benchmark from this new platform. (IBM platform announcement, IBM technical overview)
What each partner contributes
 
The first deployment pairs a 120-qubit IBM Nighthawk r2 with Umbra, using AMD GPUs and CPUs. The QSC, IBM, and AMD describe it as a shared environment where researchers can test quantum algorithms, error-correction methods, and hybrid workflows. (IBM platform announcement, AMD’s description of its role)
How quantum and supercomputing work together
Quantum computers are prone to errors. Error-correction systems repeatedly measure parts of a quantum computation; classical software, called a decoder, analyzes those measurements to infer what went wrong. That analysis has to keep pace with the quantum processor, sometimes in a feedback loop where the next quantum operation depends on the measurement just taken.
The intended workflow is:
The quantum processor runs a circuit and produces measurements.
The classical system processes those measurements and calculates likely corrections.
The system feeds results back so researchers can test the next step or round of the circuit.
Larger HPC resources can help with simulation, decoder training, optimization, and scientific analysis around the quantum work.
Keeping the quantum and classical hardware close together is meant to reduce delays and make these experiments easier to run. The IBM and AMD teams have also described earlier work using AMD GPUs for sample-based quantum diagonalization and quantum-error decoding. (IBM’s technical overview, AMD’s description)
Oak Ridge’s wider computing ecosystem
The IBM–AMD platform is one piece of ORNL’s broader effort. ORNL operates Frontier, its current exascale supercomputer, and is preparing Discovery, an HPE system powered by AMD processors and accelerators, for planned delivery in 2028. ORNL describes Discovery as part of an ecosystem combining HPC, AI, and quantum computing. The connection from the new platform to ORNL’s wider HPC environment is part of the plan; Discovery is still in development. (ORNL computing directorate, Discovery system page)
ORNL also has its own quantum systems for research. In 2026 it deployed Pathfinder, a 20-qubit IQM computer, alongside a six-qubit Quantum Brilliance system. These are separate from the IBM–AMD platform and support ORNL’s work on software and methods that can operate across different quantum hardware. (ORNL’s Pathfinder announcement)
Scientific work underway
A recent example of quantum-HPC research at ORNL is a collaboration with IBM and Cleveland Clinic that calculated nine molecular configurations of FLiBe, a molten-salt material studied for tritium production in fusion reactors. The team used a hybrid workflow to examine how tritium binds to the material at the molecular level. The result is an early computational step toward studying fusion-relevant materials; it does not establish a finished material design or demonstrate a fusion power system. The published work was described as a new paper on arXiv. (ORNL’s FLiBe report)
That work illustrates the broader approach, but it should be kept distinct from the new Umbra–Nighthawk error-correction platform: the announcement does not say the FLiBe calculations ran on that platform or used AMD’s Umbra system.
Roadmap and policy context
DOE’s Quantum Genesis initiative aims to develop scientifically relevant, fault-tolerant quantum computing capability by 2028. Its Q Competition calls for systems with at least 100 logical qubits—error-corrected qubits—and large-scale fault-tolerant operations. That target is part of the policy backdrop for the co-design platform; the new platform itself is a research environment, not a delivered fault-tolerant computer. (DOE Quantum Genesis announcement, DOE Q Competition announcement)
IBM’s own roadmap is ambitious: it announced Nighthawk r3 designs for 520 programmable qubits and 10,000 quantum operations, with a plan to connect two processors into a 1,040-qubit system in 2027. IBM says it is targeting Starling, a fault-tolerant system, for 2029. These are company plans, not current platform capabilities. (IBM Nighthawk update, IBM Starling roadmap)
Assessment
The strategic idea is straightforward: IBM supplies the quantum processor, AMD supplies much of the classical compute, and ORNL supplies the research setting and HPC expertise to test how they work together. Quantum computing has a size problem. We think cat qubits solve a big part of it 🐈‍⬛

To break RSA-2048 in about three days, we would need around 1 million standard superconducting qubits, about 33 000 m² and circa 500 MW, roughly the power consumption of Brussels 🇧🇪. With cat qubits, it's 23 000 qubits, 800 m² and 12 MW. About what an high-speed train runs on 🚄.

Why does that matter? Every qubit comes with cryogenics, wiring, control electronics and cost. A machine consuming as much as a whole city is a machine you could build, but nobody will buy. One that fits in a small building, powered by a single wind turbine, starts to look like an engineering project. 🏗️

The savings come down to physics. Cat qubits resist bit-flips by design, so error correction only has to fight phase-flips. We’ve shown this on our Boson 4 chip in 2024 and more recently on the Helium chip, where idle bit-flips times reached 1h 🧪 https://t.co/riYXCwoDig

This is a theory paper, such a machine still has to be built and the challenges to overcome are many. But a smaller machine is a much more realistic one, and arguably one that could be built sooner.

The world's transition to quantum-resistant cryptography has never been more urgent than now.

More on the findings this Wednesday in the blog post from the study's authors.👀 In the meantime, have a look at our infographic  👉 🖼️ https://t.co/Un6lNQZMsa
